quizzes.title: Module Intro: Before You Begin
quizzes.description:
MODULE INTRO
Module Intro: Before You Begin
3 questions · survey · one attempt
Instructions

Welcome to this module. This short survey is not graded for correctness. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting.

questions.text: When something becomes cheap and easy to get, do people become freer, or just more dependent? Give your best answer now. You will come back to this question at the end of the module.

This module has these goals. Read them, then choose one answer.

  • Explain how interchangeable parts, the moving assembly line, and scientific management made mass production possible.
  • Evaluate Henry Ford's strengths and weaknesses as a leader, including what his methods cost workers.
  • Describe how the automobile changed the economy and everyday life by 1929.
  • Explain how credit and the installment plan solved the problem of selling what mass production could make.
  • Compare Henry Ford's and Alfred Sloan's choices.
  • Evaluate who shared in the prosperity of the 1920s and who did not.

answers.text: I have read the goals and I understand what this module asks of me.
I have read the goals, but I have a question about one of them.

questions.text: Some assignments in this course allow you to work with classmates. How do you plan to work this module?

answers.text: I would like to work with a group when that is an option.
I would rather work on my own.
I am not sure yet.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: Ford, Credit, and the 1920s Economy
quizzes.description:
READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: Ford, Credit, and the 1920s Economy
8 questions · 8 points · one attempt
Before you start

Answer each question using what you learned in this week's two lessons. You may look back at them, but the answers are not stated word for word. You will need to put facts together.

questions.text: Ford's Five-Dollar Day paid about double the usual factory wage. Which statement best explains why it was good for his business as well as for his workers?

answers.text: It let him close the River Rouge plant and save money.
High pay cut the number of workers quitting and created customers who could afford the cars they built.
It forced his rivals to charge higher prices for their cars.
It made the assembly line unnecessary.

questions.text: Mass production made goods cheap, yet the lesson says a new problem appeared. What was it?

answers.text: Factories ran out of steel, glass, and rubber.
Workers refused to learn the new jobs.
Families stopped wanting cars and radios.
Factories could make more goods than families could pay for in cash.

questions.text: General Motors passed Ford as the top seller in 1927. Which change in the market best explains why?

answers.text: Buyers who already owned a car wanted color, style, and a better model to move up to, and Ford kept selling one plain car.
The Model T became more expensive than the cars General Motors sold.
The government began to favor General Motors.
Ford had stopped using the assembly line.

questions.text: Many families prospered in the 1920s, but a farm family in 1925 would likely have struggled to share in the boom. Which detail from the lesson best explains this?

answers.text: Farm families were not allowed to buy cars.
Farmers had paid too little in taxes.
Crop prices fell after European farms recovered, and farmers still owed debts from the boom years.
Radios did not work in the countryside.

questions.text: The Florida land boom and its collapse in 1926 is best described as an early example of what?

answers.text: A drought that ruined farmland.
A rise in prices fed by borrowed money that can fall as fast as it rose.
The success of the installment plan.
A government plan to settle new towns.

questions.text: Which action best fits the policy of laissez-faire in the 1920s?

answers.text: Leaving business mostly alone while cutting taxes and government spending.
Setting a minimum wage for every factory.
Lending government money directly to struggling companies.
Breaking up large companies to force prices down.

questions.text: Ford's Sociological Department visited workers' homes and could cut the pay of those whose habits Ford disliked. Which question does it most directly raise?

answers.text: Should factories pay their workers in cash or by check?
Can a company make more cars with fewer workers?
Should workers have a say in what their cars look like?
How far should an employer or a government go in shaping the private character of citizens?

questions.text: Older writers on republican virtue worried about a nation that lived on credit. Which of their concerns fits the lesson best?

answers.text: Credit would make goods too cheap for businesses to make a profit.
Credit would make banks too powerful to be regulated.
Credit pulls future income into the present and may weaken a people's habit of restraining its appetites.
Credit would stop families from buying American goods.

quizzes.title: Module Outro: Looking Back
quizzes.description:
MODULE OUTRO
Module Outro: Looking Back
5 questions · survey · one attempt
Instructions

You have finished this module. Please answer honestly. Your answers help your teacher see how the class is doing.

questions.text: Look back at the question from the start of the module. When something becomes cheap and easy to get, do people become freer, or just more dependent? Give your answer now, using at least one fact from this module. You may say if your thinking has changed.
How confident do you feel about the material in this module?

answers.text: Very confident. I could explain it to someone else.
Fairly confident. I understand most of it.
Somewhat unsure. I understand parts of it.
Not confident. I need help.

questions.text: What is still unclear to you? Name a person, event, or idea. If nothing is unclear, write "nothing."
Which of these did the people in this module most need, whether they had it or not?

answers.text: Courage
Courtesy
Honesty
Perseverance
Self-government
Service
Responsibility

questions.text: Pick one person from this module (Ford, Sloan, Coolidge, Mellon, or someone else) and explain, in two or three sentences, how that virtue showed up in what they did, or how its absence did.

discussions.title: Discussion: Did the Model T Make Americans Freer?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Discussion: Did the Model T Make Americans Freer?
10 points · threaded discussion
Before you start

Open the lessons "Henry Ford and the Assembly Line" and "Buying on Credit". Use My Notebook on those pages to gather your notes and marks, then come back here to post.

The question

Did the Model T, and the cheap cars and easy credit that followed it, make Americans freer? Think about workers, families, and farmers. The lessons give evidence on both sides.

Your post

Your post (about 100 to 150 words):

  1. Take a clear position: freer, less free, or freer in some ways and less free in others.
  2. Give one specific piece of evidence from this week's lessons that supports you.
  3. Name one fact that cuts against your position, and explain why you still hold it.
Your reply

Your reply (about 50 to 75 words): Respond to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with something they did not use. If not, say respectfully where their reasoning falls short.

Before you post

Post first, then reply.

Rubric
Post and reply
10.0 pts		10.0 pts Substantive
Clear position, specific evidence from the week, names a counterpoint, and the reply engages a classmate's actual reasoning		6.0 pts Thin
Position stated but evidence vague, no counterpoint, or the reply only says "I agree"		0.0 pts Missing
No post, or no reply
